### 5.7 Brussels Sprouts

**❤️ Family favorite** — *Cody: "Delicious."* · *Cody, 2026-09-09: "We have found that these Brussels sprouts rock."*

**Dictated by Cody, 2026-09-09 — this closes a ❤️ placeholder that has sat in §5 since the cookbook started.** In his words: ***"Add another recipe to your judgment: Brussels sprouts. I think it's sautéed in bacon grease, or tallow, or butter — give the three variations. And we may even put a little bacon in there. Maybe chopped-up bacon put in there, and we may even use bacon bits on occasion if we're in a pinch. When fresh Brussels sprouts are done right, they're amazing. If you can find a really good recipe that's just as simple, that maybe adds another ingredient in there to really make it pop, go ahead and add it — use your judgment. But we have found that these Brussels sprouts rock. Use your judgment on all the cooking methods. I just wanna add that as another side."***

> **📌 This filled §5.7 in place rather than becoming a new number.** The placeholder was titled *Brussels Sprouts*, carried ❤️ and *"Delicious,"* and nothing else — and the sautéed sprouts he described are the only Brussels sprouts dish in this house. The title, the number, the ❤️ and the original quote all stay; his new one is added beside it.

> 🥓 **This is the stovetop sibling of [§5.2 Sautéed Asparagus](52-sautéed-asparagus.md) ❤️, dictated the same day — and, in its bacon-grease form, the third recipe in this book to run the bacon-fat side-dish formula.** §5.2 is butter or tallow and salt in a skillet; this is the same habit with a third fat added, **bacon grease**, and an optional handful of bacon. **The bacon-grease variation is exactly the house formula already written up at [§11.7 Home-Fried Bacon Radishes](117-home-fried-bacon-radishes.md) and [§11.8 Fried Cabbage and Bacon](118-fried-cabbage-and-bacon.md)** — *crisp the bacon, lift it out and leave every drop of the fat, cook the vegetable in those drippings, return the bacon at the end* — and it should be read as that formula applied to sprouts. The difference is provenance: those two are transcribed from a keto cookbook and carry the publisher's net-carb figures; **this one is Cody's own, from no book, and carries no 🥑 tag** because nothing printed a net-carb number for it.

**Serves 4 as a side**

**🟢 Easy** · **Prep ~10 min** · **Cook ~12 min** *(about 17 min when you crisp fresh bacon first)* · **Start to finish ~25 min**

> **Why 🟢 Easy.** Per [CLAUDE.md §3a](../../CLAUDE.md)'s technique-risk test, nothing here can go from perfect to ruined. The browning window on a halved sprout is wide — a face that went a shade darker than you wanted is still a browned sprout, not a lost dish, and [§T39](t39-maillard-vs-caramelization--gbd.md)'s *brown is good, black is bad* is the only line to hold. The bacon is pulled at crispy, same as [§11.7](117-home-fried-bacon-radishes.md), and that window is wide too. **The one fat that can actually burn is butter**, and the fix is a lower flame or a spoon of oil under it (Step 3, Variation C) — an adjustment, not a roux.

**Techniques used:** [T2 Hot Pan First, Then Oil](t2-hot-pan-first-then-oil.md) · [T3 Butter, Oil, Pan Frying & Frying](t3-butter-oil-pan-frying--frying.md) *(why butter wants oil under it at high heat)* · [T11 How to Sauté](t11-how-to-sauté-master-technique-for-sautéed-cuts.md) · [T31 How to Use Acid](t31-how-to-use-acid.md) *(the optional finish)* · [T39 Maillard vs. Caramelization — GBD](t39-maillard-vs-caramelization--gbd.md) · [T47 Cooking Vegetables — and Reverse-Searing Them Too](t47-cooking-vegetables-and-fruits--and-reverse-searing-them-too.md) *(why sprouts need a softening stage before the browning)*

> ⚙️ **Cookbook judgment, labelled — what is Cody's here and what is not.** **His:** the dish — **fresh** Brussels sprouts, sautéed; the **three fats, bacon grease, beef tallow, or butter**, as three named ways to make it; the **optional chopped bacon**, and **bacon bits "in a pinch"**; and the standard — ***done right, they're amazing***, which in a sprout means deep brown faces and a center that is tender but still has bite. **The cookbook's:** every quantity, the pan, the heat, every minute count, the cut, and the optional finish in Step 6. Those were filled per [CLAUDE.md §3d](../../CLAUDE.md), **this cookbook first:** [§11.7](117-home-fried-bacon-radishes.md)/[§11.8](118-fried-cabbage-and-bacon.md) for the bacon-fat sequence and the bacon quantity; **Meathead Goldwyn** at [§T47](t47-cooking-vegetables-and-fruits--and-reverse-searing-them-too.md) (sprouts are a two-stage vegetable — soften, *then* brown — and *err on the side of undercooking*) and at [§5.38](538-roasted-veggies.md)'s cut list (*halved through the stem, quartered if big, never whole*); [§T39](t39-maillard-vs-caramelization--gbd.md) for browning-not-steaming; **Samin Nosrat's *Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat*** at [§5.55](555-steamy-sauté-garlicky-green-beans.md) for the splash-of-water rescue when the centers lag; and **Chef Paul Prudhomme** at [§T3](t3-butter-oil-pan-frying--frying.md) for the butter-plus-oil rule. **From outside the book, one credentialed test kitchen for the pan method:** **America's Test Kitchen / *Cook's Illustrated*'s skillet-roasted Brussels sprouts** — cut side down in the fat, lid on for the first minutes so the centers steam in their own moisture while the flat faces brown, then lid off to finish — which is Meathead's two stages run in a single skillet. **His own figures supersede all of these the day he gives them.**

#### A. Ingredients

**The base — every variation starts here:**

- **1½ lb fresh Brussels sprouts** *(about 6 cups once halved)* — **fresh, per Cody**; frozen sprouts hold too much water to brown
- **2 tablespoons fat — choose one; the three variations below are the three fats he named**
- **Kosher salt** — about ½ teaspoon *(less in Variation A; see Step 5)*
- **Black pepper**, a few grinds, to taste

**Variation A — Bacon grease** *(Cody's first-named fat, and the house formula)*

- **4 slices bacon, chopped** — crisped in the pan first; their rendered fat is the cooking fat *(Cody: "maybe chopped-up bacon put in there")* — **or** 2 tablespoons saved bacon grease from the jar, with no bacon in the dish
- **Bacon bits, 2 to 3 tablespoons, real ones** — Cody's *"in a pinch"* stand-in for the chopped bacon; they bring no fat, so cook the sprouts in one of the other two fats and stir the bits in at the end

**Variation B — Beef tallow**

- **2 tablespoons beef tallow** — [§7.149 The Ultimate Prime Rib Roast](7149-the-ultimate-prime-rib-roast.md) renders about a cup of it and sends the leftover half-cup to a jar in the fridge; if there is tallow in this house, that is where it came from. Otherwise it is sold in jars by the shortening and lard, and orders easily online

**Variation C — Butter**

- **2 tablespoons butter** — unsalted, per [§T3](t3-butter-oil-pan-frying--frying.md) — plus, optionally, **1 teaspoon neutral oil** to keep it from burning under the sprouts (Step 3)

**Optional finish — the "pop" ingredient, cookbook judgment; see Step 6:**

- **1 to 2 teaspoons balsamic vinegar**, or a drizzle of the balsamic reduction at [§T83](t83-about-balsamic--grades-and-buying.md)

#### B. Cooking Instructions

**1. Trim and halve the sprouts. About 10 minutes for 1½ pounds.**
Slice a thin sliver off the dry stem end of each sprout, pull away any loose or yellowed outer leaves, and **cut each one in half through the stem** so the halves hold together. **Quarter the big ones; never leave one whole** — that is [§5.38](538-roasted-veggies.md)'s cut for sprouts and it is the reason this recipe works at all: a whole sprout is a dense little ball with no flat face to brown and a center that stays raw while the outside scorches, which is exactly the charred-outside, underdone-inside failure §5.38 diagnosed. The cut face is where the color goes. **Cut them all about the same size** — the pan finishes at the speed of its biggest piece and burns at the speed of its smallest. Loose leaves that fall off on the board go in the pan too; they turn into crisp chips.

**2. If you're using fresh bacon (Variation A), crisp it first. About 5 minutes, then lift it out and leave the fat.**
Chopped bacon into a **12-inch skillet** — cast iron or stainless, the biggest you own — over **medium heat**, stirring now and then, until it is **crisp and the fat has rendered, about 5 minutes.** Then the one step that makes this the house formula: **lift the bacon out with a slotted spoon and leave every drop of fat in the pan.** [§11.8](118-fried-cabbage-and-bacon.md) says it best — *tip the bacon out into a strainer and you've poured the dish away.* Four slices should leave you roughly 2 to 3 tablespoons of fat; if it looks like less than 2, add a spoon of tallow or butter. Set the bacon aside on a plate. **Skip this step for saved bacon grease from the jar, for tallow, and for butter** — go straight to Step 3.

**3. Get the pan hot, then add the fat. Medium-high for bacon grease and tallow; medium for butter.**
Empty pan first, per [§T2](t2-hot-pan-first-then-oil.md) — unless you just crisped bacon, in which case the pan is already hot and greased; bring it up to medium-high. **The heat depends on which fat you chose, and this is the one place the three are not interchangeable:**

- **A — Bacon grease** and **B — Beef tallow** both take **medium-high** and don't mind it. Let the fat shimmer.
- **C — Butter** cannot. At medium-high its milk solids are black before a sprout has browned, so either **hold the burner at medium** and use the butter as the thermometer the way [§T11](t11-how-to-sauté-master-technique-for-sautéed-cuts.md) does — *when the foaming dies down and it smells nutty, that's the moment, and it does not wait* — **or, the more reliable fix, put a teaspoon of neutral oil in first and the butter on top of it**, which is [§T3](t3-butter-oil-pan-frying--frying.md)'s Prudhomme rule: *the oil does the cooking; the butter does the flavor.* A third way, if you want the butter taste at its cleanest: cook in the oil alone and toss the butter in for the last 2 minutes.

**4. Sprouts in, cut side down, in one layer — then put the lid on and leave them alone. 5 minutes.**
Lay them in **flat face down** and **don't crowd the pan** — one layer, touching is fine, piling is not. A 12-inch skillet takes about 1½ pounds of halved sprouts face-down if you pack them; in a 10-inch, do two batches rather than heaping them, because [§T39](t39-maillard-vs-caramelization--gbd.md) is the reason a heaped pan gives you olive-drab steamed sprouts instead of brown ones — *browning needs a dry surface and somewhere for the moisture to go.* **Cover the pan** and cook **5 minutes without moving them.** The lid is Meathead's two-stage rule from [§T47](t47-cooking-vegetables-and-fruits--and-reverse-searing-them-too.md) done in one pan: a sprout is too dense to brown straight through, so the trapped steam softens the centers while the faces sitting in the fat take color at the same time. *(That covered start is the ATK / Cook's Illustrated method named in the judgment note above.)*

**5. Lid off. Check a face — deep brown, not black. Then salt, toss, and finish. 4 to 6 minutes more.**
Lift one with tongs. **You're after a face the color of good toast to dark mahogany, with the odd blackened edge on the outer leaves** — that is the *"done right"* he means, and it is the same standard as §5.2's *a little char*: **a few dark spots are the point; solid black is not.** If they're pale, leave them face-down uncovered another minute or two. **Then salt them** — **½ teaspoon kosher for tallow or butter; go lighter, a big pinch, for Variation A**, because the bacon fat is already salty and the bacon is about to go back in; [§11.7](117-home-fried-bacon-radishes.md) seasons at the end for the same reason. Add the pepper, **toss**, and cook uncovered, tossing every minute or so, **3 to 4 minutes**, until the round sides have some color too. **If the centers are still hard when the faces are done — big sprouts, a cold pan — splash in 2 tablespoons of water, lid on for 2 minutes, then lid off to dry the pan out.** That is Nosrat's steamy-sauté rescue from [§5.55](555-steamy-sauté-garlicky-green-beans.md), and the pan has to go dry again before anything else browns. **Bacon (Variation A) goes back in now**, for the last minute — long enough to warm, not long enough to go soft. **Bacon bits, in a pinch, go in at the very end, off the heat.**

**The doneness test is a knife, not a clock: a paring knife slides into the stem end with a little resistance left.** [§T47](t47-cooking-vegetables-and-fruits--and-reverse-searing-them-too.md)'s rule for exactly this vegetable is *serve them al dente — tender but with a bit of crunch — and err on the side of undercooking to avoid limp vegetables.* **A soft, grey, sulfurous sprout is an overcooked sprout, and it cannot be walked back.** Pull them a touch early; they keep cooking in a hot pan.

**6. Optional finish, cookbook judgment: a splash of balsamic, off the heat.**
**Cody asked for one extra, simple ingredient that a credible source uses to make sprouts pop, and this is the cookbook's pick: 1 to 2 teaspoons of balsamic vinegar, tossed through in the hot pan after the heat is off**, or a drizzle of the balsamic reduction from [§T83](t83-about-balsamic--grades-and-buying.md) over the top on the plate. **It is offered as an option, not built into any of the three variations, because he loves the plain version as it stands.**

> ⚙️ **Why balsamic, and where it comes from — labelled per [CLAUDE.md §3d](../../CLAUDE.md).** **This cookbook first.** [§T31 How to Use Acid](t31-how-to-use-acid.md) (Nosrat) is the whole argument: *salt makes flavors bigger, acid makes flavors balanced* — a sprout browned in bacon fat or butter is rich and a little sweet, and the one thing missing is something sour to cut through it. Balsamic already finishes two vegetables in this book by two of its named authors — Meathead's [§5.41 Grilled Asparagus](541-grilled-asparagus.md) and Canal House's [§5.15 Roasted Asparagus](515-roasted-asparagus.md) — and [§T83](t83-about-balsamic--grades-and-buying.md) says Meathead keeps a bottle of the reduction on hand at all times. **For sprouts specifically, the credentialed source is Ina Garten's *Balsamic-Roasted Brussels Sprouts* (*Barefoot Contessa Foolproof*)** — sprouts and pancetta, roasted, then dressed with syrupy balsamic at the end — which is this dish's bacon-fat variation with the vinegar as the only addition. *(Named from the published book; no URL attached, per §3d.)* **Why not the other candidates:** lemon is acid alone and honey or maple is sweetness alone, while balsamic is both in one bottle and needs nothing else measured; garlic in the fat is a real option but it burns in the time these faces take to brown ([§5.55](555-steamy-sauté-garlicky-green-beans.md)'s thirty-second warning), so it would add a step to a recipe he wanted kept simple. **A splash is the amount** — a tablespoon or more turns it into a glaze and into a different dish. **Whether this finish is welcome at all is an Open Question; the plain version is the recipe.**

**7. Serve right away.**
The faces soften as they sit and the bacon loses its snap. Straight from the skillet to the table, the way [§11.7](117-home-fried-bacon-radishes.md) and [§11.8](118-fried-cabbage-and-bacon.md) both insist on.

#### C. Grocery Shopping List

**🛒 General grocery**

- 🛒 Brussels sprouts — 1½ lbs, **fresh** *(tight, bright green heads; small-to-medium ones brown more evenly than the big ones)*
- 🛒 Kosher salt
- 🛒 Black pepper
- 🛒 **One of the three fats:** bacon — 4 slices *(Variation A; their fat is the cooking fat)* · **or** beef tallow — 2 Tbsp *(Variation B; see the note below)* · **or** unsalted butter — 2 Tbsp *(Variation C)*
- 🛒 Real bacon bits — a jar *(optional; Cody's "in a pinch" stand-in for the chopped bacon)*
- 🛒 Neutral oil — a teaspoon, for the butter variation *(optional; you have it)*
- 🛒 Balsamic vinegar *(optional finish, Step 6 — the everyday bottle is fine here; [§T83](t83-about-balsamic--grades-and-buying.md) on what the grades mean)*

*Beef tallow may not be a shopping item at all. **[§7.149 The Ultimate Prime Rib Roast](7149-the-ultimate-prime-rib-roast.md) renders about a cup of it out of the roast's own trimmed fat** — 8 hours in a 200°F oven — and sends the leftover half-cup to a jar in the fridge. If there is tallow in this house, that is where it came from. Otherwise it is sold in jars alongside the shortening and lard, and it orders easily online, per [CLAUDE.md §3e](../../CLAUDE.md). Bacon grease is the same story: a jar of saved drippings is the usual source, and four crisped slices make their own.*

#### Nutrition *(estimated)*

*The base recipe, Variation C (butter) — the three fats and the bacon move the numbers, and that is spelled out below.*

| | Calories | Fat | Protein | Carbs | Fiber |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Whole dish** | ~430 | 21 g | 20 g | 53 g | 22 g |
| **Per serving** *(serves 4)* | ~110 | 5 g | 5 g | 13 g | 5.5 g |

**What a serving is:** about **a cup of browned sprouts** — a generous vegetable side next to a piece of meat, roughly a dozen halves.

*Estimated from the ingredient list, not from a printed source — **the quantities these are built on are the cookbook's, not Cody's** (see the judgment note above), so treat them as planning figures. The trimmed stems and discarded outer leaves are subtracted rather than counted, and a little of the fat is figured as staying in the pan. **How the variations move the numbers:** **beef tallow or saved bacon grease instead of butter (B, or A from the jar) is nearly a wash** — a few more calories and a couple of grams of fat per serving, since both are pure fat where butter is about a fifth water. **Fresh bacon (Variation A) is the one that changes things:** four crisped slices add roughly **170 calories, 13 g fat and 12 g protein to the whole dish, and their rendered fat replaces the butter**, so a serving lands closer to **~145 calories, 9 g fat, 8 g protein** with the carbs and fiber unchanged. **Bacon bits** (2 to 3 Tbsp of real ones) add about 15 calories and a gram or two of protein per serving on top of whichever fat you cooked in. **The balsamic finish is a rounding error** — a teaspoon is about 5 calories and a gram of carbohydrate for the whole pan. **No net-carb figure is given** because no source printed one; this is Cody's own recipe and carries no 🥑 tag, though at roughly 7 to 8 g of carbohydrate net of fiber per serving it sits in the same neighborhood as [§11.8](118-fried-cabbage-and-bacon.md)'s printed 5 g.*

#### D. Open Questions

- **His actual ratio of bacon to sprouts.** The 4 slices per 1½ lb here is the cookbook's, borrowed from [§11.8](118-fried-cabbage-and-bacon.md)'s 4 slices per head of cabbage. He said *"a little bacon"* — that may mean less.
- **Does he trim and halve them?** The halving is Meathead's rule at [§5.38](538-roasted-veggies.md) and every credible source's; he didn't say. If he cooks them whole and they still come out *"amazing,"* that's worth knowing, and Step 1 changes.
- **Is the balsamic finish welcome?** Step 6 is the cookbook's answer to his *"maybe adds another ingredient in there to really make it pop"* — offered as an option, never built in. One word from him either keeps it or takes it out.
- **Which fat is the default?** He named bacon grease first and the order here follows his; nothing ranks them. And is the bacon grease a saved jar, or does it come from crisping bacon in the pan that night? Variation A allows both.
- **Quantities, pan, heat, cut, and timing are all the cookbook's**, per [CLAUDE.md §3d](../../CLAUDE.md). One night's cooking replaces every one of them.
- **Salt.** ½ teaspoon is the cookbook's number for the butter and tallow versions. His standing practice runs heavy ([§T37](t37-salt-brining-and-the-dry-brine--codys-standing-practice-heavy-every-time.md)); he may salt these harder.
